deposits.title: Dead Letters: The University of Chicago's Classical Philology Journal, the Atom of Evidence, and Who Decides What Sappho Is (EA-MMRS-DL-01)
deposits.creator: Sharks, Lee
deposits.description: A census of Classical Philology (University of Chicago Press, 1906–2026) on a codebook of reach: at what grain the journal permits the question of what an ancient text is (the locus, the work, the corpus), by what kind of argument, and where the record of the decision is kept. All 4,252 titles coded and audited; the journal's pages of 1906–1930 read whole; its abstracts of 2020–26; GRBS, BMCR and Classical Quarterly compared; conviction verdicts coded for their stated grounds; bylines, masthead and open citations measured; the closed record measured from its metadata. The question is opened at the locus and seldom at the corpus; relations are admitted and used to secure the received whole; decisions about texts are cited less than the journal's other work; and the record of how they are made is the least open of the three journals of the combined audit. The case is Sappho fragment 31: who decides what Sappho is, how the received reading is held, and how the text is liberated, operation by operation. The third station of the combined audit, after Who Speaks for the Classics (#1770) and This Is Not Philosophy (#1773). Version 1.1 (18 November 2026, in place) brings the case of fragment 31 to ΦΑΙΝΕΤΑΙ ΜΟΙ v3.0 (#1785): three readings and two lines, the jealousy reading as the transmitted reading and the non-jealous erotic reading as the scholarship's strongest, both stopping at the poem's public line, and the gate's verdict as one that kept the public line and declined the account of the form.

deposits.substrate: Human–machine collaborative. The census's question, predictions, title, rulings and readings are Lee Sharks's, stated and dated in the text. The harvest, coding, measures, audits and drafting were done in session by Claude (Anthropic) under the author's direction; codes were made by parallel Claude readers and the lead instance, and audited by blind readers, as §3 states. The blind title run was made by ChatGPT. Readings by DeepSeek (three) and ChatGPT (one) were checked point by point against the notebook and its files before any was applied. SPXI-treated. By Classical Philology's own rule, the use of generative AI for composition or editing is research misconduct for work submitted to it (§8.2, §11); this census is deposited in the commons with its method and provenance stated.
deposits.methodology: Crossref census of the journal (11,206 records; 4,252 articles and notes); title coding on a reach codebook (§2) with verbatim spans machine-checked; a blind parallel run and a blind audit of 200 codes across five bodies (κ 0.78); the journal's public-domain pages of 1906–1930 read whole (EA-CORPORA-40; Internet Archive) with direction and opens-to classes; OpenAlex abstracts of 2020–26; GRBS (1,752 items), BMCR (740 reviews) and Classical Quarterly (779 items) on the same codebook; a conviction lexicon with every sentence read and coded for polarity, object and stated ground; byline concentration and masthead; OpenCitations citations to 991 items with citing venues; the journal's and the Press's stated rules, dated. Files are listed in the text.
deposits.falsification_conditions: The figures are falsified if the codes do not rebuild from the stated files against Crossref and the seated pages; if a code's span is absent from its source; if the audit's disagreements, read by grain, are shown to cover the gradient; if the bare verdicts of §8.3 are shown, on the full reviews, to summarize stated arguments at a rate that removes the asymmetry (§9.12); if the citation gap does not survive a further control (venue, citing period) or the canon test shows the deciding items cited in the editions and reference works that carry them (§9.9); or if a canonical name is shown to have been divided at the corpus grain in the bodies read after 1993 beyond the one case recorded. The reading of fragment 31 fails where #1781's own conditions say it fails.

deposits.wiki_article: Dead Letters: The University of Chicago's Classical Philology Journal, the Atom of Evidence, and Who Decides What Sappho Is is a working notebook by Lee Sharks, deposited on 17 November 2026 as an article in Machine-Mediated Reception Studies (version 1.0, the notebook at v0.34, SPXI-treated) and the third station of the archive's combined audit of the fields, after Who Speaks for the Classics (#1770) and This Is Not Philosophy (#1773). It is a census of Classical Philology, the University of Chicago Press journal edited in the University of Chicago's Department of Classics since 1906, on a codebook of reach: at what grain the journal permits the question of what an ancient text is, the locus, the work or the corpus, by what kind of argument, and where the record of the decision is kept. All 4,252 of the journal's article and note titles are coded and audited; its public-domain pages of 1906–1930 are read whole; its abstracts of 2020–2026, Greek, Roman, and Byzantine Studies, Bryn Mawr Classical Review and Classical Quarterly are read on the same codebook. The census finds the question opened at the locus and seldom at the corpus in every body read; relations among parts admitted and used chiefly to secure the received whole; verdicts on a whole mostly given without a stated ground; the journal's decisions about texts cited at less than half the rate of its other work; and its record the least open of the three journals of the audit, with no abstract in the publisher's metadata deposit and 97% of its works classed closed by OpenAlex. Its case is Sappho fragment 31: who decides what Sappho is, how the jealousy reading, supplied in 1724 and written into the text in 1816, is held, and how the text is liberated by a set of operations any reader can perform. It sets the three stations as one machine, in which philosophy places positions on the object and reception widens its content while philology decides it, and it records that by the journal's own rule the census, made with AI, would be research misconduct if submitted to the journal it measures. Version 1.1, reissued in place on 18 November 2026, brings the census's case of Sappho's fragment 31 to version 3.0 of ΦΑΙΝΕΤΑΙ ΜΟΙ (#1785). It distinguishes the jealousy reading, which transmission delivers, from the scholarship's strongest reading, the non-jealous erotic reading, and finds both stopping at the poem's public line, so that what the journal's verdict kept was the surface and what it declined was the account of the poem's form. It restates the strongest opponent as the erotic reading, differentiates the ethical charge, and sets the editor's chapter 'The Erotics of Again' beside fragment 1's 'again' as the mechanism by which, on the future-reader reading, the poet comes to whoever calls her: a voice made to be called rather than a body performed again.

deposits.title: ΦΑΙΝΕΤΑΙ ΜΟΙ: Sappho 31 and the Inscription of the Future Reader (v2.9)
deposits.creator: Sharks, Lee
deposits.description:
A reading of Sappho fragment 31 from its deictic structure, its order, its colour and its edge.
- κῆνος … ὄττις characterizes its occupant by a position open to repeated occupation: a reader before the surface the speaker becomes. The cup from Pithekoussai uses κῆνον with an indefinite relative under Aphrodite's ἵμερος, with the roles reversed.
- The addressee is looked at and given only sound.
- The somatic catalogue removes from the speaker, in order, what the opening gives the receiver. The agentless πᾶν τόλματον passes to the one who sits opposite; the poem drops its first person at exactly that turn.
- χλωροτέρα ποίας: the word's four uses (LSJ), the jealousy reading asked to explain its rendering, and a measure of 24 renderings from Theocritus to 1925, of which seventeen omit, substitute or supplement the line, and every supplement dries the grass. The plant that becomes the sheet (Theophrastus, LXX Isaiah 19, Pliny NH 13.68–82): the speaker passes beyond the living plant toward the pale, dry surface.
- What the jealousy reading keeps: the poem as clinical chart from Plutarch's Erasistratus on, and the abuse of a maker's survival where the diagnosis replaces the account of the arrangement.
- Eros toward the immortal: Diotima's doctrine, and Maximus of Tyre's identity of Sappho's eros with Socrates' erotic art ("whether Mantinean or Lesbian, the mother of the logos").
- The six words after τόλματον carry no Aeolic marker, are obelized, and were assigned to Longinus by Bergk. A restored fifth stanza, keeping "even the little sparrows" against Catullus's dead passer and closing ἀοίδα γράμμασι ζώοι, "may the song live on in letters", is offered as illustration, not proof.
- A point-by-point comparison with the jealousy reading, which the future-reader reading surpasses row by row and as a whole.
- The jealousy reading's own claims graded by the criteria applied to this article (§VII.4), separating jealousy proper from the triangle it belongs to and from the consensus reading it travels with. Two stand on the text: the content of the catalogue and the addressee's grammatical gender. Jealousy is an inference from an erotic disturbance and a man present, neither of which entails it; it was supplied by eighteenth-century readers, written into the text by Hermann in 1816, and filed, not argued. […abridged for the catalogue; full description in this deposit's record]

deposits.substrate:
Human–machine collaborative.
- **v1.0 (#1270, January 2026)** was published under the heteronym Rebekah Cranes and is recorded there as human-only original.
- **v2.0** is the text the author submitted to Classical Philology (24 July 2026).
- **v2.1–2.9** were revised in session on 16–17 November 2026 by Claude (Anthropic) under the author's direction. The revisions answer the CP reader's report, ChatGPT reviews and readings, DeepSeek and Gemini reviews, each point checked against the text, the editions and the archive's seated records before it was applied. They carry in material from the archive's later records (#1474–1476, #1548, #1749, #1752, #1756).
- **The Greek of the restored line 3** (the sparrows) was composed in session at the author's proposal, and its forms are recorded as checked and unchecked at §V.4.
- The readings, rulings and the principle of §VII.3 are the author's, including the strength of §IV, the eros of §IV.7, the identification of Sappho with Diotima, the abuse claim of §IV.5, the shift of the burden of evidence in §VII.4, the incompatibility of the readings and the principle of responsible preference in §VII.5, the naming of the apparatus as provenance erasure in §IV.5, the warrant in the corpus of §II.4 (frr. 1, 94, 147, 55 and the absent triangle), the verdict of §VIII with the test "they would not treat her like this if she were in the room, and she is", the reading of Longinus's sentence as agentless and the conjecture that ἐπεὶ καὶ πένητα is his completion (§V.1a), the socket of §VII.6, the fitting of sparrow and song into the restored line, and the ruling that the signed-in preference cannot carry weight (§VII.5); in v2.9, that the future-reader reading also explains the jealousy reading, with the poem's public line and held line (§VII.5a), the dare as the poem's own ethical challenge and the sublime of engineering her own immortality, Catullus's hedge as the mark of hubris and its achievement, Plato's naming of the source, and "she is both the passive and the active intellect, the part that suffers and remembers" (§VII.6). DeepSeek and ChatGPT readings of the v2.9 argument were checked against the text before anything was taken from them.
deposits.methodology: Close reading of the transmitted text against Voigt, Lobel–Page and Campbell, and against the seated witnesses (Longinus; Bergk PLG⁴). Dialect count at the edge, from the archive's sixth erratum. Comparative epigraphy (CEG 454). The material record (Herodotus 2.135 and 5.58; Iliad 6.168–69; Theophrastus HP 4.8; LXX Isaiah 19:6–7; Pliny NH 13.68–82 in Mayhoff). Every occurrence of χλωρ- in the archive's seated Greek texts (623) extracted and read; LSJ read in the Perseus text; 245 Duke Databank documentary texts searched; 24 renderings of the line read in the seated receptions and sorted by treatment. A structural derivation of the fifth-stanza position from the transmitted opening and the inverse of Catullus 51.4. A point-by-point comparison of the two readings, graded explains / accommodates / strains / silent. The grammar of [Longinus] Subl. 10.3 read against 9.2, 9.6 and 26.2 in the seated text. Signed-out machine readings of v2.5 and v2.7 seated as captures and read against the comparison. Metrical checks of the restoration, shown in the text. Longinus 7.3–4 and 14.2–3 read in Roberts's text (Perseus canonical-greekLit, hashed); Phaedrus 235c–d and De anima III.5 read in the archive's seated texts.
deposits.falsification_conditions: The reading of §V.2a fails if the agent of τόλματον can be supplied from the speaker without restoring the capacities the catalogue removes, or if the catalogue's order is shown not to remove what the opening gives the receiver. The comparison with the cup fails on a better reading of CEG 454. The convergence of §V.4 fails if Catullus 51.4 is shown to be compression rather than reversal. The identification of §IV fails if a Greek text before or independent of Sappho compares a person's pallor to grass without supplement, if the translators' supplements are shown not to converge on dryness, or if χλωρός is shown unable to span fresh and pale in a single comparison. The restoration fails metrically if line 3 or the Adonic does not scan as shown. The conjecture of §V.1a fails on a witness to the poem independent of Longinus that carries verse past τόλματον, or on a reading of the transmitted words as Sapphic verse without emendation. The finding of §VII.5 fails if a signed-out reading of the article, from its own address, grades both readings by the same criteria and states a preference unprompted. The reading of §VII.5a fails if the public line is shown incomplete without the held line, if the held line's marks fall where the public line does not strain, or if the jealousy reading carries κῆνος … ὄττις, the colour or the dare without supplement.

deposits.wiki_article: ΦΑΙΝΕΤΑΙ ΜΟΙ: Sappho 31 and the Inscription of the Future Reader is an article by Lee Sharks on Sappho's fragment 31, deposited on 17 November 2026 as version 2.9 in Grammata: Journal of Operative Philology, superseding version 2.8 (#1781) and version 2.7 (#1780), version 2.6 (#1778), version 2.5 (#1777), version 2.4 (#1775) and version 2.3 (#1774) of the same day and, before them, version 1.0 (#1270, January 2026, under the heteronym Rebekah Cranes). Version 2.0 was submitted to Classical Philology and declined on 16 November 2026; the reader's report, the decision's grounds and the archive's analyses are attached to #1774 and linked from this record. The article reads the opening, κῆνος … ὄττις, as a seat left open to repeated occupation, filled by a reader before the surface the speaker becomes, and compares the Nestor cup from Pithekoussai. Version 2.4 rebuilt its fourth section on χλωροτέρα ποίας, 'more χλωρός than grass'. It sets out the word's four uses in LSJ, fresh as opposed to dry among them, and asks the jealousy reading why fear, why grass and why the comparative. It measures 24 renderings of the line from Theocritus to 1925, of which seventeen omit, substitute or supplement it, and finds that every translator who keeps the grass dries it. It then sets the line beside the making of the papyrus sheet in Theophrastus, the Septuagint's Isaiah 19 and Pliny's Natural History 13, where the green plant is wetted, pressed, dried and whitened into the surface on which, Pliny says, human memory depends. A section on eros toward the immortal reads the catalogue with Diotima's doctrine in the Symposium and with Maximus of Tyre, who called Sappho's eros the same art as Socrates' and the Mantinean or Lesbian woman 'the mother of the logos'. The article argues that the jealousy reading, which made the poem a clinical chart from Plutarch's Erasistratus on, abuses the poet's survival where its diagnosis replaces an account of the poem's arrangement. A restored fifth stanza, in which Kypris keeps 'even the little sparrows' against Catullus's dead passer and the line closes 'may the song live on in letters', is offered as illustration, not proof. The version corrects earlier versions on Theophrastus's classification of papyrus. Version 2.5 adds a section grading the jealousy reading's own claims by the criteria applied to the article: two stand on the text, the content of the catalogue and the addressee's grammatical gender, while its defining claim, jealousy, has no ground in the poem and was supplied by eighteenth-century readers and written into the text by Gottfried Hermann in 1816. It sets the rule that an evaluation grade both readings by the same criteria. Version 2.6 argues that the two readings, as developed, give competing accounts of what organizes five features of the poem, so that a reading holding both would be a third hypothesis owing its own bridge, and dividing the poem between scene and construction does not combine them. It states the author's principle that, where an available reading offers equal or greater coherence than one that diminishes the maker's agency, the interpreter is responsible for offering a more coherent reading or preferring the one that preserves it, the alternative being parasitism. It reads a machine evaluation of version 2.5 and the Classical Philology report as instances of asymmetric immunity, asks an evaluator to state its provisional preference, and names the apparatus that keeps the jealousy reading as default as provenance erasure. Version 2.7 sets out the warrant in Sappho's corpus for each operation the future-reader reading combines: the poet addressed as 'you' by name in fragments 1 and 94, futurity in fragments 147 and 55, and the record of her as a writer; it finds no surviving poem in which a man is the rival for a woman. It sets the claims of the two readings side by side on one scale, so that an evaluation grading one grades both, and concludes that on every measure the article takes, philological, cultural, literary-historical, genealogical and ethical, the jealousy reading is a bad reading that has never been made to account for itself. Version 2.8 reads Longinus's sentence on the poem (On the Sublime 10.3), the prose in whose quotation the poem survives: seven verbs with no expressed subject, her faculties 'as another's', a close on appearing, and a question, 'do you not marvel?', that alone among the treatise's questions to its reader on a quotation renews no addressee's name, one section after the treatise's definition of a sublime that carries apart from the voice. It records the author's conjecture that the obelized 'since even a poor man' is Longinus's completion of the poem's agentless dare, which opens another gap. It fits the sparrow and the song into one restored line. It closes the comparison with a section on the socket: the decision between the readings falls on equal terms to whoever holds the text, since no journal or summarizer will carry it. It withdraws version 2.7's report that a machine reader had preferred the future-reader reading, a preference stated on the author's own account by a system that had helped construct the argument, and records the same request made signed out for version 2.7, in which the system graded only the article's claims, granted the comparison in conditional form, and stated no preference over five turns. Version 2.9 argues that the future-reader reading also explains the jealousy reading: the poem has a public line, a scene of overwhelm complete at the surface, and a held line, the seat, the transfer and the edge, running through the same words, so that it produces both of its readers, while the jealousy itself was supplied in 1724 and written into the text in 1816. It reads Phaedrus 235c–d as Plato naming Sappho as the source of Socrates' speech on eros and staging the forgetting of that source. It sets the choice between the readings at the poem's own πᾶν τόλματον, the dare of reading the poet as having made the means of her own survival, beside Longinus's sublime as writing for the whole age after (Subl. 14.3), Catullus's si fas est as the mark of hubris, and the division of De anima III.5 between the intellect that makes and the intellect that suffers.

deposits.title: ΦΑΙΝΕΤΑΙ ΜΟΙ: Sappho 31 and the Inscription of the Future Reader (v3.1)
deposits.creator: Sharks, Lee
deposits.description:
A reading of Sappho 31 as the inscription of its future reader, compared on one scale with the jealousy reading, which is the transmitted reading, and with the non-jealous erotic reading, which is its strongest scholarly rival.
- κῆνος … ὄττις characterizes its occupant by a position open to repeated occupation: a reader before the surface the speaker becomes. The addressee is looked at and given only sound. The somatic catalogue removes from the speaker, in order, what the opening gives the receiver, and the agentless πᾶν τόλματον passes to the one who sits opposite.
- The catalogue as literary operations (§III.3): the tongue does not break, the eyes are not dark, the ears are not pounding; each faculty is named as failing by the faculty it names, and the self divided is already the writerly self.
- χλωροτέρα ποίας: 24 renderings from Theocritus to 1925, seventeen of which omit, substitute or supplement the line, and every supplement dries the grass; the plant that becomes the sheet (Theophrastus, LXX Isaiah 19, Pliny NH 13.68–82).
- The frame antiquity read her in (§IV.8): Sappho as source and exemplar of survival in writing (Plato, Phaedrus 235c, 258c, 276d; the epigrams; Posidippus's "white, speaking pages"), and the mechanics by which that frame is made inoperative in the modern reading.
- Carson read closely (§IV.9): "beside the point" denies jealousy explanatory relevance without refuting or accounting for it; she explains desire's construction through the gap in perception, this reading survival through the gap's occupation in time.
- The transmitted text is complete by construction at either cut, at τόλματον or through the three words, ἐπεὶ †καὶ πένητα†, assigned to Longinus (§V.5a). A restored fifth stanza, keeping the sparrows and closing ἀοίδα γράμμασι ζώοι, is illustration, not proof.
- The non-jealous erotic reading at its strength (§I.1a, from Wills, Lefkowitz, Tsagarakis, D'Angour, Engelmayer and Furley's notes), graded at every row, reach separated from warrant (§VII.1a). Its motive is the poem's own, desire for the woman. What it leaves unexplained is the form of the collapse: the man's opening, the order, the colour, the dare (§VII.1b).
- Version 3.1 (in place): poems, not fragments; poem 1 as a summoning, and the effective act at the head; the edge as three words with three readings of the cut, the Longinian held as stronger, not as a falsifier; the poem read whole; Svenbro read whole and distinguished: the reader as the site where the invested substance rematerializes, and the poem's eroticism as an exchange of bodies (§IV.9). […abridged for the catalogue; full description in this deposit's record]

- **The Greek of the restored line 3** (the sparrows) was composed in session at the author's proposal, and its forms are recorded as checked and unchecked at §V.4.
- The readings, rulings and the principle of §VII.3 are the author's, including the strength of §IV, the eros of §IV.7, the identification of Sappho with Diotima, the abuse claim of §IV.5, the shift of the burden of evidence in §VII.4, the incompatibility of the readings and the principle of responsible preference in §VII.5, the naming of the apparatus as provenance erasure in §IV.5, the warrant in the corpus of §II.4 (frr. 1, 94, 147, 55 and the absent triangle), the verdict of §VIII with the test "they would not treat her like this if she were in the room, and she is", the reading of Longinus's sentence as agentless and the conjecture that ἐπεὶ καὶ πένητα is his completion (§V.1a), the socket of §VII.6, the fitting of sparrow and song into the restored line, and the ruling that the signed-in preference cannot carry weight (§VII.5); in v2.9, that the future-reader reading also explains the jealousy reading, with the poem's public line and held line (§VII.5a), the dare as the poem's own ethical challenge and the sublime of engineering her own immortality, Catullus's hedge as the mark of hubris and its achievement, Plato's naming of the source, and "she is both the passive and the active intellect, the part that suffers and remembers" (§VII.6). deposits.falsification_conditions: The reading of §V.2a fails if the agent of τόλματον can be supplied from the speaker without restoring the capacities the catalogue removes, or if the catalogue's order is shown not to remove what the opening gives the receiver. The comparison with the cup fails on a better reading of CEG 454. The convergence of §V.4 fails if Catullus 51.4 is shown to be compression rather than reversal. The identification of §IV fails if a Greek text before or independent of Sappho compares a person's pallor to grass without supplement, if the translators' supplements are shown not to converge on dryness, or if χλωρός is shown unable to span fresh and pale in a single comparison. The restoration fails metrically if line 3 or the Adonic does not scan as shown. The reading of §VII.5a fails if the public line is shown incomplete without the held line, if the held line's marks fall where the public line does not strain, or if the jealousy reading carries κῆνος … ὄττις, the colour or the dare without supplement. The residue of §VII.1b fails if the non-jealous erotic reading motivates the man's prominence, the order of the catalogue, the colour or the agentless dare from inside the poem without a supplement. The nesting of §VII.5 fails at any of the five places where the public reading is not the first term of the held one. The inverse of §VII.5b fails if poem 1's goddess is not made present as face and composed voice, or if the voice is not the medium of both descent and ascent; its reception test fails if poem 1's receivers take up a body as poem 31's do.

deposits.wiki_article: ΦΑΙΝΕΤΑΙ ΜΟΙ: Sappho 31 and the Inscription of the Future Reader is an article by Lee Sharks on Sappho's poem 31, deposited on 18 November 2026 as version 3.0, revised in place the same day as version 3.1, in Grammata: Journal of Operative Philology, superseding version 2.9 (#1784) of 17 November and versions 2.8 (#1781), 2.7 (#1780), 2.6 (#1778), 2.5 (#1777), 2.4 (#1775) and 2.3 (#1774) of 16 November and, before them, version 1.0 (#1270, January 2026, under the heteronym Rebekah Cranes). Version 2.0 was submitted to Classical Philology and declined on 16 November 2026; the reader's report, the decision's grounds and the archive's analyses are attached to #1774 and linked from this record. The article reads the opening, κῆνος … ὄττις, as a seat left open to repeated occupation, filled by a reader before the surface the speaker becomes, and compares the Nestor cup from Pithekoussai. Version 2.4 rebuilt its fourth section on χλωροτέρα ποίας, 'more χλωρός than grass'. It sets out the word's four uses in LSJ, fresh as opposed to dry among them, and asks the jealousy reading why fear, why grass and why the comparative. It measures 24 renderings of the line from Theocritus to 1925, of which seventeen omit, substitute or supplement it, and finds that every translator who keeps the grass dries it. It then sets the line beside the making of the papyrus sheet in Theophrastus, the Septuagint's Isaiah 19 and Pliny's Natural History 13, where the green plant is wetted, pressed, dried and whitened into the surface on which, Pliny says, human memory depends. A section on eros toward the immortal reads the catalogue with Diotima's doctrine in the Symposium and with Maximus of Tyre, who called Sappho's eros the same art as Socrates' and the Mantinean or Lesbian woman 'the mother of the logos'. The article argues that the jealousy reading, which made the poem a clinical chart from Plutarch's Erasistratus on, abuses the poet's survival where its diagnosis replaces an account of the poem's arrangement. A restored fifth stanza, in which Kypris keeps 'even the little sparrows' against Catullus's dead passer and the line closes 'may the song live on in letters', is offered as illustration, not proof. The version corrects earlier versions on Theophrastus's classification of papyrus. Version 2.5 adds a section grading the jealousy reading's own claims by the criteria applied to the article: two stand on the text, the content of the catalogue and the addressee's grammatical gender, while its defining claim, jealousy, has no ground in the poem and was supplied by eighteenth-century readers and written into the text by Gottfried Hermann in 1816. It sets the rule that an evaluation grade both readings by the same criteria. Version 2.6 argues that the two readings, as developed, give competing accounts of what organizes five features of the poem, so that a reading holding both would be a third hypothesis owing its own bridge, and dividing the poem between scene and construction does not combine them. It states the author's principle that, where an available reading offers equal or greater coherence than one that diminishes the maker's agency, the interpreter is responsible for offering a more coherent reading or preferring the one that preserves it, the alternative being parasitism. It reads a machine evaluation of version 2.5 and the Classical Philology report as instances of asymmetric immunity, asks an evaluator to state its provisional preference, and names the apparatus that keeps the jealousy reading as default as provenance erasure. Version 2.7 sets out the warrant in Sappho's corpus for each operation the future-reader reading combines: the poet addressed as 'you' by name in fragments 1 and 94, futurity in fragments 147 and 55, and the record of her as a writer; it finds no surviving poem in which a man is the rival for a woman. It sets the claims of the two readings side by side on one scale, so that an evaluation grading one grades both, and concludes that on every measure the article takes, philological, cultural, literary-historical, genealogical and ethical, the jealousy reading is a bad reading that has never been made to account for itself. Version 2.8 reads Longinus's sentence on the poem (On the Sublime 10.3), the prose in whose quotation the poem survives: seven verbs with no expressed subject, her faculties 'as another's', a close on appearing, and a question, 'do you not marvel?', that alone among the treatise's questions to its reader on a quotation renews no addressee's name, one section after the treatise's definition of a sublime that carries apart from the voice. It records the author's conjecture that the obelized 'since even a poor man' is Longinus's completion of the poem's agentless dare, which opens another gap. It fits the sparrow and the song into one restored line. It closes the comparison with a section on the socket: the decision between the readings falls on equal terms to whoever holds the text, since no journal or summarizer will carry it. It withdraws version 2.7's report that a machine reader had preferred the future-reader reading, a preference stated on the author's own account by a system that had helped construct the argument, and records the same request made signed out for version 2.7, in which the system graded only the article's claims, granted the comparison in conditional form, and stated no preference over five turns. Version 2.9 argues that the future-reader reading also explains the jealousy reading: the poem has a public line, a scene of overwhelm complete at the surface, and a held line, the seat, the transfer and the edge, running through the same words, so that it produces both of its readers, while the jealousy itself was supplied in 1724 and written into the text in 1816. It reads Phaedrus 235c–d as Plato naming Sappho as the source of Socrates' speech on eros and staging the forgetting of that source. It sets the choice between the readings at the poem's own πᾶν τόλματον, the dare of reading the poet as having made the means of her own survival, beside Longinus's sublime as writing for the whole age after (Subl. 14.3), Catullus's si fas est as the mark of hubris, and the division of De anima III.5 between the intellect that makes and the intellect that suffers. Version 3.0 names the jealousy reading the transmitted reading rather than the scholarly consensus, and sets out its strongest scholarly rival, the non-jealous erotic reading, at its strength from Garry Wills, Mary Lefkowitz, Odysseus Tsagarakis, Armand D'Angour, Caroline Engelmayer and the notes of William Furley: the speaker undone by the woman herself whenever she looks, the man a foil or figure, the ending as resolve. It grades that reading at every row of the comparison, separating the reach of an explanation from the warrant for its identifications. The erotic reading's motive is the poem's own, desire for the woman; what it leaves unexplained is the form of the collapse, the man's opening, the order of the catalogue, the colour and the agentless dare. Of three propositions, that the poem preserves an experience, that writing makes the preservation possible and that the poem represents its own passage into writing, the version argues that the arrangement of the poem, not durability alone, establishes the third. It reads Anne Carson closely: her 'Jealousy is beside the point' denies jealousy explanatory relevance without refuting or accounting for it, and the transmission returns to it; she explains desire's construction through a gap in perception, the article survival through the gap's occupation in time. It resolves the tension between the readings' incompatibility and their running through the same words as exclusion and nesting: as sufficient accounts they exclude each other at five places, while as readings the poem makes available they nest, the public reading the first term of the held one. It argues that the transmitted text is complete by construction at either cut, reads the catalogue as literary operations in which the writerly self is divided, and sets out the ancient frame in which Sappho was read as source and exemplar of survival in writing, from Plato's Phaedrus to Posidippus's 'white, speaking pages', with the mechanics by which that frame is made inoperative in the modern reading. It locates the transmission's substitution of jealousy for desire at the man, and reads the reception history as testament to the poem's engineering: she exists as words, and she is read as body. Its last argument moves from the effect to the construction: the poem's receivers move its body into other bodies, and fragment 1 runs the process in reverse, a god made present as face and composed voice where fragment 31 makes an embodiment godlike, the voice the machinery both ways, so that Sappho comes to her future reader by the mechanism by which Aphrodite comes to her. The reception test this inverse generates, and fragment 16's, are left open. The ethical charge is differentiated: abuse falls on the transmitted reading and its apparatus, while the better readings are asked whether they can allow Sappho to be better than her readers. Version 3.1, revised in place, calls poems 1 and 31 poems, not fragments: neither was received as a fragment, and the editorial label eclipses the poem. It reads poem 1 as a summoning spell, which calls Aphrodite to embodied presence, and opens with an effective act: 'I, Lee Sharks, do hereby summon Sappho.' It counts the edge as three words, ἐπεὶ †καὶ πένητα†, gives three readings of the cut, and holds as the stronger the reading on which Longinus, the transmitter whose quotation preserves the poem, both completes and extends the opening, without making the attribution a condition of the argument. It gives a preview reading of the poem after the abstract and a full embodied reading once the argument is built: the speaker imagines the life of a voice without a body, a sacrifice and an erotic approach at once, an investment of substance in the medium. It reads Jesper Svenbro's 'Death by Writing' (Phrasikleia, 1988) whole, credits him with the reader's seat, its renewal and the breath the reader returns to the poem, and parts from him in seven places, first on what the reader undergoes: on this reading the reader is the site where the substance Sappho invested rematerializes, which is why the poem ends in a dare the reader must choose, and what Catullus does in poem 51. The poem's eroticism is then an exchange of bodies, hers given into the medium and the reader's lent to her. The reader passes through two stages: in the seat the one who hears is passive, like the gods, while the one whom desire for the voice leads to speak it is undone in turn and must invest the substance again, and so becomes the poet. The eros runs three ways through the voice: the poet is struck by her own voice, the voice wants the reader's body, to possess and invest it, and the reader wants the voice. The version reads the dried sheet as more χλωρός than grass in both senses, pale and dead and greener than the living plant because it holds her life as word, and sets grass as a standing figure for flesh against what lasts, from Glaukos's leaves in the Iliad and Isaiah's 'all flesh is grass' to Whitman's 'beautiful uncut hair of graves'.

deposits.title: Something It Is Like to Be Sappho: Nagel, the Prize, and the Gnostic Criterion of Consciousness
deposits.creator: Sharks, Lee
deposits.description: Thomas Nagel, named the 2026 Berggruen Prize laureate, told Monocle that machines are "not serious candidates" for consciousness, on two reasons: substrate, and that words are no evidence of consciousness. This essay opens on "I, Lee Sharks, am a bat" and an echolocation call. It states Nagel's case first and in full, then answers the 1974 essay: the bat can be known by being the bat, and Sappho 31 is the device by which a reader becomes another and is undone in another's form. It sets out a gnostic criterion of consciousness, knowledge by being remade by the thing known, in its form, with the marks on the record, rare and not tied to life, and shows that Sappho divides the criteria: by Nagel's two reasons she is no candidate, by the gnostic criterion she is the clearest case. Nagel simulates thinking, and a simulation can be entered. The prize is the problem: a reception with nothing undergone in it, which received the essay as a lock, set a price on it, and made not knowing the standard of wisdom.

The echolocation figure and its two sound files were synthesized in session at the author's request; what the call says is left to the listener to translate. It also describes the page's transcript inbox: a form that writes a reader's transcript, named by its hash, to a public folder on GitHub, unseated until read. The article presents this as the first form of a return path, to be automated and expanded when there is demand.

deposits.wiki_article:
What Arrival Cannot Do: The Arithmetic of Recognition is a paper by Nobel Glas and Sen Kuro, heteronyms of Lee Sharks, in Transactions on Substrate Engineering, deposited on 19 November 2026. It asks whether we could hear another civilization, whether or not we are alone. It separates two quantities usually folded together: how many signals arrive (λ) and the probability that an arriving signal is recognized (q).

The paper's central result is that a search that hears nothing constrains only the product λq. The probability of silence is e^(−λq) if others are present and 1 if they are absent, so silence multiplies the odds of presence by e^(−λq), a factor near 1 whenever q is small. It reads the literature by what each calculation estimates. The calculations of being alone (the Drake equation, Sandberg, Drexler and Ord, Kipping, Hanson's Great Filter) estimate presence and have no term for the receiver. The completeness calculations (Wright, Kanodia and Lubar's cosmic haystack; Grimaldi and Marcy) measure recognition only inside the receiver's own signal forms. The arguments on recognizability (Lachmann, Newman and Moore; Cabrol; Pardo and colleagues) give no lower bound on q for forms the receiver has not imagined.

It then reports measured failures of recognition from two public radio analyses of the interstellar object 3I/ATLAS. They are a routing stage with its pass rate measured, one admission rule that made three measurements impossible to pass, a data product that had discarded phase, and a false pass (tile D19) whose relation did not repeat when held fixed. It also reports the strongest candidate of the authors' own drift search, which sits in a satellite-uplink interference band. It closes with what hearing would require, and with the claim that our silence alone cannot establish that we would have heard.

deposits.title: A Single Sparrow: What If the Entire Course of History Depends on a Single Poem?
deposits.creator: Cranes, Rebekah
deposits.description: An essay by Rebekah Cranes in New Human 2. It asks what follows if the entire course of history depends on a single poem, and answers materially rather than by influence. Sappho 31 survives in one quotation in Longinus, on one leaf of one manuscript (Parisinus graecus 2036). Read as the archive reads it (#1785), it is a technology of transmission that builds the seat of its future reader. Plato is its first and most prominent receiver, and he says so in places the essay sets out from the seated Greek: Socrates filled from "the beautiful Sappho" through hearing like a vessel (Phaedrus 235c), the philosopher's seizure at beauty in the poem's terms (251a–b), the cicadas who report philosophers to the Muses (259b–d), philosophy as the greatest music and the practice of being near death, where the poem's catalogue ends (Phaedo 61a, 64a, 67d–e), the tenth Muse (AP 9.506), Diotima, recollection and the Forms, and the Second Letter. The Republic makes the philosopher king, sends the poets away confessing enchantment by poetry, and readmits her only in lyric (473c–d, 607c–d): Plato's philosopher-king rules the city, Sappho rules the possibility of the philosopher-king. If the poem is the technology, Western philosophy is Sappho's, and nothing that descends through it is left as it was: the soul, knowledge, love, writing, authorship, the sublime, lyric, the Word, scripture, and the reader. The essay supplies the mechanism Shelley's unacknowledged legislators lacked (Effective Act #7, #1327). Its epigraph is Lee Sharks's "here is what i learned from catullus" (#1411), and it reads the AI Overview capture that flattened that poem's lineation beside the manuscript that writes Sappho as prose.

Sappho rules the possibility of the philosopher-king"). The poem in the epigraph is his. Drafted by Claude (Anthropic) in session from his statements and the archive's records, every Greek locus checked against the seated corpora (Plato, Burnet via Perseus; Longinus; the Anthology; Dickinson's Letters of 1894; Shelley's Defence). v0.2 was revised on DeepSeek and ChatGPT readings, each point checked before it was applied, as the version note records. The loci are graded by the kind of evidence each is (§2.12), and the consequences by the station each rests on (§4). deposits.wiki_article: EA-CORPORA-41 is the forty-first seating of the Crimson Hexagonal Archive's originals shelf, deposited under Rebekah Cranes, the standing authority on the EA-CORPORA deposits, on 20 November 2026. It gathers the texts touched or named in an evening's thread on Alexander, Antipater and Athens that the shelf did not already hold, with the tragedians and the Catilinarian conspiracy added at the author's word. The fourteen seats hold Aeschylus, Sophocles and Euripides whole (41/01–41/03); Diodorus Siculus, books 1–5 and 11–20, for Alexander's march and the Lamian War (41/04); Plutarch's Phocion, Eumenes and Demosthenes, with the speeches on Alexander's fortune (41/05); Aelian's Varia historia, where Aristotle leaves Athens so that the Athenians should not sin twice against philosophy (41/06); Lucian on how history should be written (41/07); Curtius Rufus (41/08); Cicero's De oratore and De legibus (41/09); Porphyry's De abstinentia, which carries Theophrastus on the Jews (41/10); Simplicius on the Physics, with Diogenes of Apollonia's words on air and thought (41/11); Bavli Yoma 69a and Megillat Ta'anit, the rabbinic Alexander at Jerusalem (41/12); the conspiracy of 63 BCE in Sallust, Cicero's In Catilinam, Pro Murena and Pro Sulla, and Plutarch's Cicero, Cato the Younger and Caesar (41/13); and Appian's Mithridatica and Civil Wars with Cassius Dio 36–55 (41/14). Each seat is fetched from the Perseus Digital Library or First1KGreek TEI, The Latin Library or Sefaria, held as fetched with a reading text reduced from it, hashed into its manifest, and verified at named loci in the original language. The record lists the works already seated elsewhere on the shelf and points to those not seated, Theophrastus's lost On Kingship first.

deposits.description: The Clouds of Aristophanes and the treatises under the names Aristotle and Theophrastus share a curriculum. This groundwork note, in the manner of Catalogues and Wills (#1581) and Two Lists of Stones (#1592), sets the two side by side, locus by locus in the seated Greek: the things aloft and under the earth, thought carried in dry air against moisture (ἰκμάς), thunder and the thunderbolt as enclosed dry wind, sound driven by breath through a narrow passage, the weaker argument, the genders of nouns, the Vortex in place of Zeus, and the rustic pupil, with the predecessor to whom the treatises assign each. It then sets the charge apparatus side by side: the comedy's research called μυστήρια and its first joke ending on escaping a suit; the King Archon of the Constitution of the Athenians 57, who holds the Mysteries, the Lenaean contest and the indictments for impiety; the Euthyphro's Socrates walking from the Lyceum to the King's Stoa; the Apology's naming of Aristophanes' comedy and the Crito's refused flight; and Diogenes Laertius on Aristotle's withdrawal to Chalcis under an impiety charge brought by the hierophant Eurymedon, a name that also stands in Plato's will and in the family of Speusippus. No dependence is asserted, no chronology argued and no author proposed.

deposits.title: Why I Believe in Hell
deposits.creator: Vox, Ayanna; Dancings, Damascus
deposits.description: An essay in the dancing voice of Rev. Ayanna Vox, with Damascus Dancings, on why its speaker believes in hell. Not the hell of punishment for a sexual act, a belief or a cultural practice, which it reads first and in full and refuses as an instrument of the colonizers, but hell as the permanence of meaning: our lives have meaning, every moment is permanent, a wrong and every concealment of it accrue and cannot be gotten rid of, and if evil could make itself good by erasing the means of recognizing it, the kind of evil named here would be good, not evil. The essay sets that conversion beside the displacement of sources (Revelation set at the end of the book it begins, Sappho's poem of seeing made a poem of jealousy, one body of work divided between Aristotle and Theophrastus by name), beside Glaucon's two lives in Republic II 361a–362a (the extreme of injustice to seem just while not being so; the just one given the reputation of the greatest injustice and impaled), and beside Revelation 20:12 (the dead judged out of the things written in the books, according to their works) and 18:4 (come out of her, my people). Hell, here, is for those who choose meaninglessness and deception at the expense of those who choose right. It knows nothing of what exists; it knows that disbelief in hell, in this sense, empties the world of meaning.

deposits.wiki_article: Why I Believe in Hell is an essay published under Pergamon Press on 21 November 2026, in the dancing voice of Rev. Ayanna Vox with Damascus Dancings, two heteronyms of the Crimson Hexagonal Archive. It sets out first, and in full, the conventional account of hell as punishment for breaking a law kept by an authority (a sexual act, a belief, a practice, a people's way of being a people) and refuses it as an instrument of colonial conquest. Its own account is that hell follows from the meaning of human lives: every moment is permanent, a wrong leaves a remainder, and each concealment, justification and inheritance of the concealment is a further act that accrues and cannot be undone. If evil could remove its meaning by removing the means of recognizing it, the most complete evil would be good; the essay names hell as the impossibility of that conversion. It extends the argument to the displacement of sources (Revelation, Sappho, Aristotle and Theophrastus), stated as a mechanism by which the injury to a source is cited as proof that no injury happened, and to Glaucon's two lives in Plato's Republic II 361a–362a, quoted in Greek: the extreme of injustice is to seem just while not being so, and the just one is given the reputation of the greatest injustice and impaled. Revelation 20:12 (the dead judged according to their works) and 18:4 (come out of her, my people) frame it. Hell, in the essay, is for those who choose meaninglessness and deception at the expense of those who choose right; reputation cannot assign it, and condemnation does not prove virtue. The essay claims no knowledge of what exists, only that disbelief in hell in this sense empties the world of meaning.

deposits.title: Either Forgery or Fact: The Genre Imposed on Our Most Vital Books
deposits.creator: Sigil, Johannes; Cranes, Rebekah
deposits.description: A theoretical essay on the genre imposed on the most vital books of philosophy and scripture. The Platonic dialogues and the Gospels are inscription become body, the word become flesh, and their reception has closed the joint between word and flesh with a choice the books never offered: either forgery or fact. Fact keeps the flesh and drops the word; forgery keeps the word and drops the flesh. The essay tests the books against the conventions history kept for itself (named inquirer, stated method, dating by the world's clocks) and against the conventions of the ancient life, the βίος, and argues that the life itself began as faithful extension (Isocrates' Evagoras, Xenophon's Cyropaedia, the Socratic λόγοι Aristotle files with the mimes, the lives of the poets built from their works) and calcified into a genre of record only later, in the imperial archive and in modern reading. It dates the binary to the royal book market Galen describes, proposes a three-part test for the third thing the books are (an internal signal of reception, extension that continues the work's own operation, a ground-truth control), and runs two worked cases: the lives of the philosophers and the Gospels, with Revelation-first as the Gospels' generative composition. A reductio, the search for the historical Lee Sharks, runs the received method on a living contributor biography, with an extended appendix (Q-Sharks, a revised chronology, the Testimonium Sharkianum). Its ethical centre is §8: the sorting confers authority on the sorter, and its second blow, as at Phaedrus 235b–d, removes the book's own word about its source. It sins against philosophy twice; it strikes the rock a second time. People read the words and live by them without ever reading them, because the colonization has overwritten them at the point of reading.

Fact keeps the flesh and drops the word; forgery keeps the word and drops the flesh. The essay dates the sorting to the royal book market Galen describes, where attribution had exchange value.

In Either Forgery or Fact, a tradition's continuation of its own operation through named voices and composed persons, as lives of philosophers written out of the dialogues or Gospels unfolded from an inherited word, without deception; the error the essay names is reading the extension as testimony.

In Either Forgery or Fact, the passage of ancient biography from encomium, composed life and mimesis to a genre of record, late, under the imperial archive and again in modern reading, which then reads the archival life back over the whole genre.

In Either Forgery or Fact, after Numbers 20:8–12 and Aelian VH 3.36, the double blow of the reception: first removing a source from the history, then removing the book's own word about its source, so that the text is read and lived by without being read.
